analysis.one_liner: Doubles and sets minimum fines and prison terms for oil spills and water pollution.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise oil-spill penalties was introduced by Rep. Ted Lieu with 5 cosponsors, referred to committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Water Act to raise both the floor and the ceiling on civil fines for oil spills, and to double criminal fines and prison terms for illegal discharges — for example, doubling the top penalty for knowing violations from $250,000 and 15 years to $500,000 and 30 years. It would also change "up to" penalties to "at least" penalties, so polluters could no longer be fined token amounts. It never left the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishermen, and taxpayers who currently absorb the damage and cleanup costs of oil spills would benefit if spills become costlier for the companies that cause them. Higher minimum and maximum fines, plus longer prison terms, give regulators and prosecutors more leverage against offshore oil and shipping operators, and give coastal residents more deterrence against spills like the 2021 Orange County pipeline leak that prompted the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Raises civil penalties for oil spills by changing them from 'up to' a maximum to 'at least' a minimum, so polluters can no longer settle for token fines
Doubles criminal fines and prison terms for illegal discharges — the top penalty for knowing violations goes from $250,000 and 15 years to $500,000 and 30 years, and everyday fines double as well
Doubles the fines and imprisonment terms for negligent and repeat violations under the Clean Water Act's enforcement provisions

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas producers, pipeline operators, and shipping companies that discharge oil or hazardous substances would bear higher fines and longer criminal exposure when they pollute. Some of those costs could ultimately reach consumers through higher prices, though the bill imposes no new tax or fee.

drawbacks.text: Converting civil penalties from 'up to' an amount to 'at least' an amount removes judicial discretion and could impose disproportionately large fines on small violators or minor, accidental discharges

Higher compliance and liability costs for offshore operators and shippers could be passed through to consumers in the form of higher fuel and shipping prices, an objection oil and shipping interests would raise
The bill changes penalty levels only; it does not add new inspection, monitoring, or prevention requirements, so it addresses punishment after a spill rather than stopping spills before they happen

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — making oil pollution genuinely expensive for the companies that cause it instead of leaving coastal communities and taxpayers to absorb the damage — is real and squarely serves the public. The strongest objection is the loss of discretion from minimum mandatory fines, which is a fair design concern but a narrow one; the pass-through of costs to consumers is modest since the bill affects only violators. On balance a reasonable, if narrow, public-interest bill whose main flaw is that it punishes spills rather than preventing them.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee — later in a subcommittee — for the rest of the Congress and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on November 12, 2021 with four California Democratic cosponsors, following the October 2021 Orange County oil pipeline spill off the California coast
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced, and on November 24, 2021 to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and pipeline operators and marine shippers are better off, because the penalties they would have faced for spills were never enacted. No member ever had to cast a recorded vote on it.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise oil-spill penalties

for.name: Reps. Brownley, Porter, Levin, and Lowenthal

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Peter DeFazio, D)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup was scheduled after it was referred, including after it was sent to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no record of who supported or opposed it on the floor; all six sponsors were California Democrats.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas producers and pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would have doubled the civil and criminal penalties they face for spills and set minimum fines, directly raising the cost of the pollution they cause. Its defeat leaves the existing, lighter penalty structure in place.
Shippers that discharge oil or hazardous substances into U.S. waters would have faced doubled fines and prison terms under the Clean Water Act amendments.
